title: To school when old
hookLine: Seneca goes to lectures as an old man: learn as long as you don't know (Letters 76)
carry: learn as long as I live

lines: A BUILDING MORE CROWDED THAN SCHOOL.
cards: Five days in a row now, a man long past his student years has gone to a philosopher's school in Naples and sat through the afternoon lecture. The lecturer is named Metronax. The student is Seneca.
In the seventy-sixth letter he reports it to Lucilius, and he can already hear the teasing coming back: at your age? He answers it before Lucilius can finish the joke.
And on the way to class, he passes a building far more crowded than the school.

teach.b: Seneca puts the teasing in Lucilius's mouth himself: at your age! He doesn't deny his age.

teach.h: LEARN AS LONG AS YOU DON'T KNOW.
teach.b: He turns the question around: what could be sillier than refusing to learn because you haven't learned for a long time? Then his rule.
Learning should last as long as your ignorance lasts: tamdiu discendum est, quamdiu nescias. And if we believe the proverb, he adds, that means as long as you live.
There's never a day when you've finished not knowing something.

teach.h: THE THEATER FULL, THE SCHOOL EMPTY.
teach.b: On his way to the lecture, Seneca passes the theater of Naples, packed to the rafters. People crowd in to hear a flute player, or to decide who's the better musician.

The philosopher's school has only a handful of listeners, and the crowd thinks those few have nothing better to do. Seneca finds this a little sad, and a little funny. He isn't saying an old person needs to catch up.

teach.h: A STUDENT'S POSTURE, A LIVING MIND.
teach.b: The posture of a student is the posture of a living mind.

teach.h: LEARN AS LONG AS I LIVE.
teach.b: Seneca on his fifth day of class is a quiet answer to anyone who thinks they're too old, too busy or too established to begin something new.

how: People who take Seneca's advice keep learning at any age, coming to a new subject as a beginner without apology.

games.q: you're long past your student years, and a friend teases you for going back to school. what does Seneca do?
o: hire a private tutor so no one sees.
keep going: learn as long as you don't know.
games.why: Seneca went five days running and wrote that we should keep learning as long as we live.

practice: Think of something you've told yourself you're too old, too late or too settled to learn, and notice what that too-old voice sounds like, and whose it might be.
Then picture yourself as Seneca on his fifth day of class, unbothered by the teasing, and ask what the first small lesson would be.

wordCard.voice: Metronax. The philosopher whose lectures Seneca sits through in old age, proving his own rule: learn as long as you don't know, which means as long as you live. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin, Seneca, Letters 76.3: one must keep learning as long as one doesn't know.
